carousels.name: 5 things partners should know about men and p*rn (IFS 2024)

slides.title: 5 things partners should know [[about men and p*rn.]]
slides.sub: About 1 in 10 adults under 40 watch daily. Men are about twice as likely as women.

slides.title: [[Daily]] users
slides.body: An Institute for Family Studies / YouGov survey of 2,000 adults under 40 (2024) found about 10% watch p*rn at least once a day — and men were about twice as likely as women to be daily users.

slides.title: Know [[1–2]]
items: It's common — but common doesn't mean it's fine for your relationship.
It's usually not about you. Many men use p*rn to escape stress or boredom.

slides.title: Know [[3–5]]
items: Hiding is often shame, not a lack of love.
Quitting is hard — slips can happen even when he means it.
You're allowed boundaries about what you'll accept.

slides.title: If it's [[happening]]
items: Talk calmly — ask, don't accuse.
Get support for yourself too.
Look at actions, not just promises.
Encourage real help — a counselor, a program.

slides.title:

carousels.name: 6 questions partners ask about his p*rn problem, answered

slides.title: 6 questions partners ask [[about his p*rn problem — answered.]]
Q [[1–2]]
items: "Is it my fault?" No. P*rn addiction isn't caused by your body or your effort.
"Is it cheating?" Couples decide that together — but secrecy breaks trust either way.

slides.title: Q [[3–4]]
items: "Can he actually stop?" Many people do, usually with support and a plan.
"Should I check his phone?" It may calm you short-term, but it makes you the police.

slides.title: Q [[5–6]]
items: "Will it get better?" Often, if he's honest and doing the work.
"What about me?" Your feelings matter. Get support of your own.

slides.title: You're not [[alone]]
slides.body: Many partners of people with p*rn problems go through this quietly. A counselor or a friend you trust can help you decide what's right for you.
